t:
(a) 
The Secretary of the Treasury shall strike and furnish to the California Institute of the Arts not more than one hundred thousand duplicate copies of such medal in bronze. The medals shall be considered as national medals within the meaning of section 3551 of the Revised Statutes (31 U.S.C. 368).
 
    (b) 
The medals provided for in this section shall be made and delivered at such times as may be required by the California Institute of the Arts in quantities of not less than two thousand. The Secretary of the Treasury shall cause such medals to be struck and furnished at not less than the estimated cost of manufacture, including labor, materials, dies, use of machinery, and overhead expenses, and security satisfactory to the Director of the Mint shall be furnished to indemnify the United States for full payment of such costs.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that an outside entity, the California Institute of the Arts, directs the timing of delivery, which could look like coordination with a non-federal party. But the Institute is only a recipient and purchaser ordering duplicate medals and reimbursing costs; it has no say in the design or any federal policy decision. Nothing in the section provides for consultation, a hearing, comment, rulemaking, an advisory body, or a right to sue.
fable.s: The medals provided for in this section shall be made and delivered at such times as may be required by the California Institute of the Arts in quantities of not less than two thousand.

qwen_block.w: This section authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to manufacture and deliver medals to a specific institution. It does not require the Secretary to consult with the California Institute of the Arts or any other outside party before making the decision to strike the medals; rather, it mandates the action itself. The reference to the Institute is as the recipient of the goods, not as a participant in the decision-making process.
qwen_block.s: The Secretary of the Treasury shall strike and furnish to the California Institute of the Arts not more than one hundred thousand duplicate copies of such medal in bronze.

opus.w: The California Institute of the Arts only orders duplicate bronze copies of a medal whose design is already set, chooses delivery timing, and pays the full cost of manufacture. That is a purchase arrangement, not consultation with an outside party before a federal decision. The tempting 'Yes' reading draws on Example 10, but there the outside board determined the medal's emblems and inscriptions. Here the outside party has no say in any policy or design decision.
opus.s: The medals provided for in this section shall be made and delivered at such times as may be required by the California Institute of the Arts in quantities of not less than two thousand.
opus.b:
The obvious argument for "Yes" is that this looks like Example 10. There, an outside advisory board both determined the medal's "emblems, devices, and inscriptions" and set delivery times. Here, the California Institute of the Arts, a private body outside the federal government, sets when medals are made and delivered: "at such times as may be required by the California Institute of the Arts."

That reading fails against the definition. In Example 10, the Yes rested on the outside board shaping the content of a federal decision, the medal design. Here the medal design ("such medal") is fixed elsewhere. The Institute only orders duplicate copies, chooses delivery timing in lots of at least two thousand, and pays the full cost with security posted. That makes the Institute a buyer placing an order, not a party consulted before a federal decision is made. This is closer to the excluded categories (contracts, applications) than to an advisory or consultative role. Because timing control could still be read as outside input, I hold this at moderate confidence.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes the production and delivery of medals to a specific outside entity (the California Institute of the Arts). While the Institute specifies delivery times, this is a logistical detail for the fulfillment of a statutory mandate, not a participatory process in a federal decision. The definition excludes applications for benefits or grants, and this interaction is analogous to a recipient receiving an authorized benefit or product, rather than consulting on a policy decision.
qwen_chat.s: The Secretary of the Treasury shall strike and furnish to the California Institute of the Arts not more than one hundred thousand duplicate copies of such medal in bronze.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the California Institute of the Arts (an outside entity) is "participating" because the Secretary must furnish medals "at such times as may be required by" the Institute. This sounds like coordination or consultation.

Why it fails: The definition explicitly states that participation does not include "applications for benefits or grants." This section authorizes the production and delivery of medals to a specific institution. The Institute's role is essentially that of a recipient or customer specifying delivery logistics, not a participant in a federal decision-making process (like rulemaking, advisory boards, or public hearings). The interaction is administrative/logistical regarding the fulfillment of a statutory authorization, not a consultative process for a government decision. The Institute is not helping the government decide *whether* or *how* to make a policy; it is simply receiving the product authorized by Congress.
